title: Acids, bases and pKa
goals: Recognise amines, alcohols, ethers, thiols, sulfides and ammonium ions, and say which are Lewis bases
Rank bases using the periodic trends: stronger to the left in a row and going up a column
Recall the lecture's pKa values from HI (−10) to an alkane (50 to 60)
Explain a difference in acidity by naming what stabilizes the conjugate base
Predict which side of an acid-base equilibrium is favoured from two pKa values

sections.title: The functional groups of Chapter 6, and Lewis acids and bases
sections.html:
Chapter 6 opens with six functional groups built on nitrogen, oxygen and sulfur. R stands for any carbon group.

NameGeneral formulaExample
amines{{R-NH2}}[[mol:CCN]]
alcohols{{R-OH}}[[mol:CCO]]
ethers{{R-O-R}}[[mol:CCOCC]]
thiols{{R-SH}}[[mol:CCS]]
sulfides{{R-S-R}}[[mol:CCSCC]]
ammonium{{R-NH3+}}[[mol:CC[NH3+]|me]]

Notice the pattern. Thiols and sulfides are the sulfur versions of alcohols and ethers: sulfur sits directly below oxygen in the periodic table. An ammonium ion is what an amine becomes when its nitrogen takes up a proton.

The lecture then names the idea that organizes the rest of the course, Lewis acids and bases:

  • A Lewis base donates an electron pair.
  • A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair.

The first five groups in the table all have lone pairs, on N, O or S, so all of them can act as Lewis bases. Losing or gaining a proton is one kind of Lewis acid-base reaction: the base uses a lone pair to make a bond to H. The rest of this lecture is about how strongly different bases hold on to that proton.

micro.t: Why the ammonium ion is the odd one out
micro.h: Draw the Lewis structure of each group and count lone pairs on the heteroatom. An amine nitrogen has one. The oxygen of an alcohol or ether has two, and so does the sulfur of a thiol or sulfide. The nitrogen of {{R-NH3+}} has none: all four of its electron pairs are in bonds, which is why it carries a positive charge. With no lone pair to give, an ammonium ion cannot be a Lewis base. It is the conjugate acid of the amine, and it gives a proton back easily. Keeping the amine and its ammonium ion apart matters for one of the exam's {{pKa}} traps.

macro.t: The same six groups in proteins
macro.h: These groups are the reactive parts of amino acid side chains. Serine has an alcohol, cysteine a thiol, methionine a sulfide, and lysine an amine that is present as its ammonium ion at the pH of the body. Whether such a group is protonated or not decides its charge, and so how a protein folds and what it binds. In this course the same groups return as nucleophiles in the substitution lectures: HS− and HO− on 11/03 and 11/05, and the thiolate that builds a ring in Question 6B of the past exam.

why.q: An amine is a Lewis base but an ammonium ion is not. Why?
why.a: A Lewis base must donate an electron pair. The nitrogen of an amine has a lone pair to give. In the ammonium ion that pair is already used in the fourth N-H bond, so the nitrogen has nothing left to donate. The ion acts as an acid instead.

sections.title: Base strength on the periodic table: increasing to the left and going up
sections.html:
The lecture sketches a corner of the periodic table, C, N, O in one row with P and S below, and draws two arrows on it:

  • Basicity increases to the left across a row.
  • Basicity increases going up a column.

Four anions put the arrows to work:

{{HS-}} < {{HO-}} < {{H2N-}} < {{H3C-}}: increasing base strength

{{HS-}} is below {{HO-}} in the same column, so it is the weaker of those two. Then {{HO-}}, {{H2N-}} and {{H3C-}} run from right to left across the row, getting stronger at each step. {{H3C-}} is the strongest base of the four.

The lecture then writes the conjugate acid under each base. A base and its conjugate acid are tied together: the stronger the base, the weaker its conjugate acid.

Base{{HS-}}{{HO-}}{{H2N-}}{{H3C-}}
Base strengthweakeststrongest
Conjugate acid{{H2S}}{{H2O}}{{NH3}}{{CH4}}
Acid strengthstrongestweakest

So acid strength increases in the opposite direction: {{H2S}} is the strongest acid of the four and {{CH4}} the weakest. An acid is strong when the base it leaves behind is stable and content to keep its electrons.

micro.t: The reasons behind the two arrows
micro.h: Across a row the atoms are about the same size, and what changes is electronegativity. Oxygen holds a negative charge more comfortably than nitrogen, and nitrogen more comfortably than carbon. A comfortable anion is a weak base, so basicity rises toward the left, where the atom holds its charge least well. Down a column the change is size. Sulfur is larger than oxygen, so the charge of {{HS-}} is spread over a bigger volume and is more stable. A more stable anion is a weaker base, so basicity rises going up. Both reasons are on the lecture's list of six factors.

macro.t: Basicity and nucleophilicity do not follow the same arrows
macro.h: On 11/05 the same sketch of the periodic table returns with a second pair of arrows: basicity increases to the left and up, but nucleophilicity increases to the left and down. {{HS-}} is a weaker base than {{HO-}} and yet a better nucleophile (relative rates 126,000 and 16,000). The past exam tests exactly this in Question 1C: circle the stronger nucleophile of {{HS-}} and {{HO-}}, and of {{I-}} and {{Cl-}}. Learn the basicity trend here as a statement about holding a proton, and keep it separate from the speed of attack on carbon.

why.q: Why is the methyl anion the strongest base of the four?
why.a: Carbon is the least electronegative of C, N and O, so it is the atom least able to stabilize a negative charge. The methyl anion is therefore the least stable of the anions and the most eager to share its electron pair with a proton. Its conjugate acid, methane, is correspondingly the weakest acid.

sections.title: pKa: the definition and the numbers to memorize
sections.html:
Acid strength is measured with an equilibrium. For any acid H-A:

H-A ⇌ {{H+}} + {{A-}}, with equilibrium constant {{Ka}}, and {{pKa}} = −log {{Ka}}

A strong acid has a large {{Ka}} and so a low {{pKa}}. Each {{pKa}} unit is a factor of 10 in acid strength.

These are the values the professor wrote, from the strongest acid to the weakest:

Acid{{pKa}}Conjugate base
H-I−10{{I-}}
H-Br−9{{Br-}}
H-Cl−8{{Cl-}}
{{H3O+}}−1.5{{H2O}}
{{CF3CO2H}}−1.5{{CF3CO2-}}
H-F4{{F-}}
{{R-CO2H}}4{{R-CO2-}}
{{H2O}}15.7{{HO-}}
R-OHabout 16{{RO-}}
H-C≡C-H25{{HC≡C-}}
{{RNH2}}38{{RNH-}}
R-H (alkane)50 to 60{{R-}}

These are the values the exam expects. A few differ from the usual tables, which give about 3.2 for HF, about 0 to 0.5 for {{CF3CO2H}} and −1.7 for {{H3O+}}. Write the lecture's numbers.

micro.h: {{pKa}} = 4 means {{Ka}} = 10−4: in water, a carboxylic acid gives up its proton only slightly. {{pKa}} = −9 means {{Ka}} = 109: HBr gives up its proton completely. To compare two acids, subtract. A carboxylic acid (4) and an alcohol (16) differ by 12 units, so the carboxylic acid is 1012 times stronger. Water (15.7) and an alkane (50) differ by about 34 units. The scale covers about 70 powers of ten, which is why approximate values are enough: the exam asks for approximate {{pKa}} values, and being right to the nearest unit or two earns the points.

The 38 in the table is for a neutral amine acting as an acid: {{RNH2}} losing one of its N-H protons to give {{RNH-}}. That almost never happens, because {{RNH-}} is a very strong base. The number about 10 to 11 that appears in many tables belongs to a different acid, the ammonium ion {{R-NH3+}}, losing a proton to give back the neutral amine. Before writing a {{pKa}}, look at what is drawn. If the structure is a neutral amine, the acidic hydrogen is the N-H and the answer is about 38.

macro.t: Question 1A asks for five of these
macro.h: Question 1A of the past exam (15 points) shows five compounds and asks for the approximate {{pKa}} of each: phenol 10, pentane about 50, ethanol 16, propyne 25 and diethylamine 38. Four come straight from this table. Diethylamine is the trap described above. For propyne the acidic hydrogen is the one on the triple-bond carbon, not a {{CH3}} hydrogen. Phenol is not on the lecture's list: its value of 10 lies far below an alcohol's 16 because the negative charge of the conjugate base is shared with the ring by resonance.

macro.t: pKa decides how a drug travels in the body
macro.h: Most drugs are weak acids or weak bases, and their {{pKa}} decides whether they are charged at a given pH. An acid is mostly un-ionized when the pH is below its {{pKa}} and mostly ionized when the pH is above it. Aspirin is a carboxylic acid with a {{pKa}} of about 3.5. In the stomach, at a pH of about 2, much of it is the neutral acid, which passes through cell membranes easily. In blood, at pH 7.4, nearly all of it is the charged carboxylate. The same reasoning is used for every acidic or basic drug.

why.q: Why does a lower pKa mean a stronger acid?
why.a: A strong acid dissociates more, so its equilibrium constant Ka is larger. Because pKa is the negative logarithm of Ka, a larger Ka gives a smaller, or more negative, pKa. Each unit lower is ten times more dissociation.

sections.title: What stabilizes a base: induction, and the list of six factors
sections.html:
Why are the numbers what they are? The lecture's answer is always the same: look at the conjugate base. Anything that stabilizes the base {{A-}} makes the acid H-A stronger.

The first example compares an ordinary carboxylic acid, {{pKa}} 4, with trifluoroacetic acid, {{pKa}} −1.5:

[[mol:CC(=O)O]] [[mol:OC(=O)C(F)(F)F]]

The conjugate base {{CF3CO2-}} is stabilized by induction. The three fluorine atoms are strongly electronegative and pull electron density toward themselves through the sigma bonds. That draws some of the negative charge away from the carboxylate oxygens and spreads it over more of the ion. A more stable base means a stronger acid.

The lecture then lists the factors that stabilize a base:

FactorHow it stabilizes the baseExample
Inductionnearby electronegative atoms pull charge through bonds{{CF3CO2H}} −1.5, {{R-CO2H}} 4
Sizea larger atom spreads the charge out{{H2S}} 10, {{H2O}} 15.7
Hybridizationmore s character holds the pair closer to the nucleusH-C≡C-H 25, {{CH3CH3}} 60
Aromaticitythe base is an aromatic ioncyclopentadiene, about 16
Resonancethe charge is shared by several atoms{{R-CO2H}} 4, R-OH 16
Electronegativitya more electronegative atom holds the charge better{{H2O}} 15.7, {{NH3}} 38, {{CH4}} 50 to 60

The lecture works through induction, hybridization and size in detail.

micro.t: How large is the inductive effect here?
micro.h: The two acids differ by 4 − (−1.5) = 5.5 {{pKa}} units, so {{CF3CO2H}} is 105.5, about 300,000 times, stronger than the ordinary acid. In energy, each {{pKa}} unit is worth 1.36 kcal/mol at 25 °C (RT × 2.303, with RT = 0.592), so the three fluorines stabilize the conjugate base by about 5.5 × 1.36 = 7.5 kcal/mol relative to its acid. Induction works through sigma bonds and fades quickly with distance: it is strongest when the electronegative atoms are on the carbon next to the charged group, and it adds up, so three fluorines do more than one.

micro.t: A common mistake: explaining the acid when you should explain the base
micro.h: A weak answer says that the fluorines make the O-H bond weaker, or make the hydrogen more positive. The reasoning the lecture wants, and the reasoning that earns the points, compares the two conjugate bases. Write both anions, say which is more stable and name the factor: {{CF3CO2-}} is more stable than {{CH3CO2-}} because of induction, so {{CF3CO2H}} is the stronger acid. The same three-part sentence (draw the bases, pick the more stable, name the factor) works for every acidity comparison in this course.

macro.t: Resonance, the factor behind two exam answers
macro.h: Resonance was not worked through in this lecture, but it is on the list and the past exam leans on it. A carboxylic acid (4) is 12 units stronger than an alcohol (16) because the carboxylate shares its charge equally between two oxygens. That is why acetate is a weak base, which is the key to Question 7A: with 2-bromopropane, acetate substitutes while the much stronger base ethoxide eliminates. Phenol's {{pKa}} of 10 in Question 1A has the same cause, a charge shared with the ring. Resonance also makes tosylate a good leaving group in Question 2A.

why.q: Why does stabilizing the conjugate base make the acid stronger?
why.a: Acidity is the position of the equilibrium between H-A and its ions. Lowering the energy of the conjugate base lowers the energy of the product side, so the equilibrium shifts toward dissociation and Ka increases. The acid has not changed: its base has become a better place for the electrons to be.

sections.title: Hybridization: why acetylene (25) is far more acidic than ethane (60)
sections.html:
Both of these acids lose a proton from carbon, yet they differ by 35 {{pKa}} units:

Acid{{pKa}}Conjugate baseHybridization of the carbon that holds the lone pair
H-C≡C-H (acetylene)25acetylide, {{HC≡C-}}{{sp}}
{{H3C-CH3}} (ethane)60ethyl anion, {{CH3CH2-}}{{sp3}}
[[mol:C#C]]

The same element carries the charge in both conjugate bases, so electronegativity and size cannot be the explanation. The difference is the orbital the lone pair sits in.

The lecture's note on the acetylide carbon: {{sp}}, more s character, more stable anion.

  • An {{sp}} orbital is half s and half p: 50% s character.
  • An {{sp3}} orbital is one part s and three parts p: 25% s character.

An s orbital is closer to the nucleus than a p orbital of the same shell. The more s character a hybrid orbital has, the closer its electrons are held to the positive nucleus, and the more stable a lone pair in that orbital is. The acetylide lone pair, in an {{sp}} orbital, is held tightly. The ethyl anion's lone pair, in an {{sp3}} orbital, is held loosely, which makes it one of the strongest bases there is.

The order to remember: {{sp}} C-H (25) is more acidic than {{sp2}} C-H, which is more acidic than {{sp3}} C-H (50 to 60).

micro.t: A carbon that behaves as if it were more electronegative
micro.h: One way to hold this idea is to say that an {{sp}} carbon acts like a more electronegative atom than an {{sp3}} carbon. It is the same element with the same nuclear charge, but its bonding and lone-pair orbitals are pulled in closer, so it keeps electrons more tightly. The {{pKa}} values show how large the effect is. On the lecture's scale an alkyne C-H at 25 lies between an alcohol O-H (16) and an amine N-H (38). So a carbon acid can be stronger than a nitrogen acid, which the electronegativity trend alone would never predict.

macro.t: The alkyne C-H on the past exam, and why 25 is a useful number
macro.h: In Question 1A of the past exam the {{pKa}} of propyne is 25, and the answer requires knowing that the acidic hydrogen is the one on the triple-bond carbon, not one of the three {{CH3}} hydrogens, which sit on an {{sp3}} carbon. The value 25 is low enough to be practical. A base whose conjugate acid has a higher {{pKa}}, such as the amide ion (38), removes that proton completely. The product, an acetylide ion, is a carbon nucleophile, and it appears at the top of the nucleophile table in the 11/05 lecture with a relative rate of 126,000.

why.q: The negative charge is on carbon in both acetylide and the ethyl anion. Why is acetylide so much more stable?
why.a: The lone pair of acetylide is in an sp orbital, which has 50% s character, while the lone pair of the ethyl anion is in an sp3 orbital with 25% s character. Electrons in an orbital with more s character are closer to the nucleus and lower in energy. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid.

sections.title: Size: why hydrogen sulfide (10) is more acidic than water (15.8), and three acids in a row
sections.html:
The next comparison is {{H2S}}, {{pKa}} 10, against {{H2O}}, written on this page as 15.8. Oxygen is more electronegative than sulfur, so electronegativity would predict that water is the stronger acid. It is not. The lecture's explanation is about the conjugate base {{HS-}}:

The larger atom “spreads out” the charge → more stable.

Sulfur is in the third row and is much larger than oxygen. The same single negative charge is spread over a larger volume in {{HS-}} than in {{HO-}}. A charge that is spread out is more stable than one that is concentrated, so {{HS-}} is the more stable, weaker base, and {{H2S}} is the stronger acid. (The lecture uses 10 for {{H2S}}, and that is the value for this exam. Most tables give about 7.)

The lecture then lines up three acids in a row:

Acid{{pKa}}Conjugate baseMain reason the base is stable
{{H2S}}10{{HS-}}size of sulfur
acetic acid, {{CH3CO2H}}4acetate, {{CH3CO2-}}resonance over two oxygens
HBr−9{{Br-}}size of bromine

Reading across: as the acids get stronger from left to right in the notes, their conjugate bases get weaker. {{HS-}} is the strongest base of the three and {{Br-}} is the weakest by a wide margin.

micro.t: When to use size and when to use electronegativity
micro.h: The two factors point in opposite directions down a column, so you need a rule for which one wins. Across a row, the atoms are similar in size and electronegativity decides: {{CH4}}, {{NH3}}, {{H2O}} get more acidic toward the right. Down a column, the change in size is large and size decides. The halogen acids in the lecture's list show it: HF 4, HCl −8, HBr −9, HI −10. Fluorine is the most electronegative element, yet HF is by far the weakest of the four, because fluoride is the smallest ion and holds its charge in the most concentrated form.

macro.t: Weak bases are good leaving groups
macro.h: The stability of an anion matters beyond acid-base reactions. In a substitution, the leaving group departs with an electron pair, so a group leaves easily when it is a stable, weak base. The 11/05 lecture uses these same numbers: bromide (conjugate acid −9) is a good leaving group, hydroxide (conjugate acid 15.7) is a strong base and a poor one, and fluoride (HF about 4) is not a good one. In biology, the thiol of the amino acid cysteine is noticeably more acidic than the alcohol of serine, for the reason given here: sulfur is larger than oxygen.

why.q: Oxygen is more electronegative than sulfur. Why is H2S nevertheless a stronger acid than H2O?
why.a: Oxygen and sulfur are in the same column, where the change in atomic size outweighs the change in electronegativity. Sulfur is much larger, so the negative charge of HS− is spread over a bigger volume and is more stable than the concentrated charge of HO−. The more stable conjugate base belongs to the stronger acid.

sections.title: Solvent effects: solvation stabilizes a base, and the gas phase reverses the order
sections.html:
So far every explanation has looked at the anion alone. The solvent matters too. Table 6.8, p. 247 gives the {{pKa}} of water and four alcohols in solution:

Acid{{pKa}} in solution
{{H2O}}15.7
{{CH3OH}}15.5most acidic
{{CH3CH2OH}}15.9
{{(CH3)2CHOH}}16.5
{{(CH3)3COH}}17.0least acidic

Among the alcohols, the more carbon groups on the carbon that carries the OH, the weaker the acid. But in the gas phase the relative acidity runs the other way: acidity increases down this list, and tert-butanol is the most acidic.

The lecture explains the solution order by drawing the two extreme conjugate bases with solvent molecules around them:

[[mol:C[O-]|me]] [[mol:CC(C)(C)[O-]|me]]
  • {{CH3O-}} is small. It is surrounded by many solvent molecules: more solvation.
  • {{(CH3)3CO-}} has a larger nonpolar group, so fewer solvent molecules can gather around the charged oxygen: less solvation.

The rule: solvation → stabilization. Methoxide is better solvated, so it is the more stable base in solution, and methanol is the stronger acid. tert-Butoxide is poorly solvated, less stable and a stronger base.

micro.t: What solvation is, and why the gas phase is different
micro.h: In water or an alcohol, the solvent's O-H hydrogens carry a partial positive charge. They point at the negative oxygen of an alkoxide and form hydrogen bonds to it, and each of those contacts lowers the energy of the ion. Three bulky {{CH3}} groups around the oxygen of tert-butoxide block some of those contacts. In the gas phase there is no solvent at all, so the only thing that can stabilize the charge is the ion itself. A larger alkyl group has more electrons that can shift a little toward or away from the charge, which spreads it out. That favours tert-butoxide, so the order reverses.

macro.t: tert-Butoxide and solvation return in the substitution lectures
macro.h: This table explains two things about tert-butoxide that the past exam uses. It is a slightly stronger base than methoxide (17.0 against 15.5), and it is bulky, which makes it a poor nucleophile (11/05 lecture). Question 1C asks which of {{(CH3)3CO-}} and {{CH3O-}} is the stronger nucleophile, and the answer is methoxide, although it is the weaker base. Solvation itself comes back as the solvent effect on reaction rates: a solvent that surrounds a nucleophile slows it down, and in Question 6A the solvent DMSO leaves an alkoxide unsolvated and very reactive.

why.q: tert-Butanol is the least acidic alcohol in solution but the most acidic in the gas phase. How can both be true?
why.a: In solution the deciding factor is solvation: the bulky tert-butyl group keeps solvent molecules away from the charged oxygen, so tert-butoxide is the least stabilized anion. In the gas phase there is no solvent, and the larger alkyl group, which can spread the charge within the ion, gives the most stable anion. Acidity depends on the surroundings as well as on the molecule.

sections.title: Predicting equilibria from pKa, and how strong a base the methyl anion is
sections.html:
The lecture ends by using {{pKa}} values to predict which way a proton transfer goes. Write the {{pKa}} under the acid on each side. The equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid, the one with the higher {{pKa}}.

Water (15.7) and hydroxide give hydroxide and water (15.7). The acid is the same on both sides, so K = 1:

[[eq:O + [OH-]>>[OH-] + O]]

Water (15.7) and the amide ion give hydroxide and ammonia (38). Ammonia is by far the weaker acid, so the equilibrium lies to the right:

[[eqr:O + [NH2-]>>[OH-] + N]]

Ammonia (38) and the methyl anion give the amide ion and methane (50 to 60). Methane is weaker still, so this also lies to the right:

[[eqr:N + [CH3-]>>[NH2-] + C]]

Put the three lines together and they form a ladder: {{H3C-}} can take a proton from ammonia, {{H2N-}} can take one from water, and neither reverse reaction happens to any useful extent.

The lecture closes with a question and an answer. {{CH4}} → {{H3C-}}? That would be a very strong base, the conjugate base of an acid with {{pKa}} 50 to 60. No ordinary base can make it by pulling a proton off methane. The answer written beside it is {{Li-CH3}}: a strong base. A carbon bonded to lithium behaves like {{H3C-}}, which is the subject of the next chapter.

micro.t: Putting a number on “lies to the right”
micro.h: For an acid-base reaction, K = 10 raised to the power ({{pKa}} of the acid formed − {{pKa}} of the acid used). Water with the amide ion: 10(38 − 15.7) = 1022.3. Ammonia with the methyl anion: 10(50 − 38) = 1012 at the least. Water with hydroxide: 100 = 1. In energy, each unit of {{pKa}} difference is 1.36 kcal/mol at 25 °C, from {{dG}} = −RT ln K with RT = 0.592 kcal/mol. The first reaction is downhill by 22.3 × 1.36 = about 30 kcal/mol. A common slip is to subtract the wrong way round. Check the sign against the rule: the side with the weaker acid must come out favoured.

macro.t: The same comparison decides substitution against elimination
macro.h: Comparing two {{pKa}} values is the most reused calculation in this unit. It tells you whether a base is strong enough to remove a given proton, which decides whether E2 can compete with {{SN2}}. In Question 7A of the past exam, the rubric gives 10 points for tying basicity to the {{pKa}} of the conjugate acids: acetate (acid 4) is a weak base and substitutes, ethoxide (acid 16) is a strong base and eliminates. In Question 1D the same reasoning explains why acid is added only after the Grignard reagent has reacted: a carbanion would take a proton from any acid at once.

why.q: Why can the methyl anion not be made by treating methane with hydroxide?
why.a: Methane has a pKa of 50 to 60 and water, the acid that would be formed, has a pKa of 15.7. The equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid, which is methane, by a factor of at least 10 to the power 34. Hydroxide is far too weak a base, so chemists make carbon-metal bonds another way, from an alkyl halide and a metal.

summary: Amines, alcohols, ethers, thiols and sulfides have lone pairs and are Lewis bases, and an ammonium ion is the conjugate acid of an amine.
Basicity increases to the left across a row and going up a column: HS− < HO− < H2N− < H3C−, and the acids H2S, H2O, NH3, CH4 run the opposite way.
pKa = −log Ka, and a lower pKa means a stronger acid: HI −10, HBr −9, HCl −8, H3O+ −1.5, CF3CO2H −1.5, HF 4, RCO2H 4, H2O 15.7, ROH about 16, HC≡CH 25, RNH2 38, alkane 50 to 60.
To explain acidity, compare the conjugate bases: induction, size, hybridization, aromaticity, resonance and electronegativity each stabilize a base.
CF3CO2H is a stronger acid than RCO2H by induction, acetylene (sp) is stronger than ethane (sp3) by hybridization, and H2S is stronger than H2O by size.
In solution a small alkoxide is better solvated and more stable, so methanol (15.5) is more acidic than tert-butanol (17.0), and the order reverses in the gas phase.
An acid-base equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid, the one with the higher pKa.
The methyl anion is a very strong base (conjugate acid pKa 50 to 60), and methyllithium behaves like it.
